title: Charting the Maritime Fuel Transition
gist: BCG and GCMD model maritime fuel mixes to 2050 and find carbon pricing is decisive: new fuels need IMO penalties near $700/t CO2e, while regional-only rules leave fossil fuels at 85%. No single fuel wins, so owners, ports and investors should preserve flexibility.

themes.theme: Carbon price as the decisive lever

insights.claim: Alternative maritime fuels (biofuels and e-fuels) still cost two to three times as much as conventional VLSFO on a production-cost basis, and the gap widens once logistics, handling and opportunity costs are included.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Without a policy subsidy, fuel switching is uneconomic; capex timing hinges on regulation.

insights.claim: Under the proposed IMO Net Zero Framework agreed at MEPC 83, new fuels only become cost competitive when the most restrictive penalty, the Tier 2 Remedial Unit, approaches $700 per ton of CO2e.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: $700/t is the breakeven policy level to watch for demand-pull on green fuels.

insights.claim: Uncertain regulation and fuel economics together stall investment across the maritime fuel chain: shipowners hesitate on new-fuel engines, ports on bunkering infrastructure without assured demand, and producers and investors on scaling supply.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: A circular demand-signal deadlock; a clear global price would unlock it.

insights.claim: Disagreement among nations has left a patchwork of rules and carbon pricing mechanisms, including the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime at regional level, complicating long-term planning.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Regional fragmentation raises compliance complexity and cost uncertainty.

insights.claim: In the base case, with the IMO penalty at $380 per ton of CO2e, VLSFO still makes up 25% of the 2050 fuel mix.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Even a sizable penalty leaves fossil fuel a significant share.

insights.claim: If only regional pricing mechanisms take effect, fossil fuels supply 85% of 2050 shipping energy, with just 4% of that mitigated by onboard carbon capture.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Failure of global agreement means little change in the fuel mix.

insights.claim: In the high-penalty scenario, with NZF penalties rising gradually to $700 per ton by 2050, fossil fuel use is lowest and a large share is mitigated by onboard carbon capture and storage.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Carbon capture on conventional ships is a key beneficiary of high penalties.

insights.claim: Conventional engines without OCCS would be 19% of fleet engine capacity in 2050 under the high-penalty scenario versus 37% under regional regulation.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Shows engine-stock sensitivity to policy outcome.

insights.claim: In the high-penalty scenario new fuels capture about 60% of fleet energy demand.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Upside case for alt-fuel producers and infrastructure.

insights.claim: No scenario produces a single dominant fuel by 2050; the mix stays fragmented across fuel types and bunkering locations.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Avoid single-fuel bets across the value chain.

insights.claim: Base-case hydrogen is about $3/kg by 2050; a fall to about $2/kg, driven by scale and cheaper renewable power and electrolyzers, would boost new fuels such as e-methanol and e-ammonia in the 2050 mix.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Electrolyzer and renewable power costs are the upstream swing factor.

insights.claim: E-methanol cost is highly sensitive to biogenic CO2 cost, tested between $50 and $200 per ton, as well as to LCOH.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Biogenic carbon supply is a bottleneck input.

insights.claim: Early cuts in biomethanol production cost would spur dual-fuel methanol-capable newbuilds, creating installed engine capacity that lowers the barrier to later e-methanol uptake.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Biomethanol is a stepping stone that builds the e-methanol market.

insights.claim: Ethanol is about 9% of 2050 energy in the base case but is very sensitive to regulatory treatment; classifying food-crop biofuels as equal to fossil fuels would curtail its use.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Ethanol outcome is a regulatory binary.

insights.claim: The levelized cost of e-methanol and e-ammonia per unit of energy is near parity, because ammonia's production-cost advantage is largely offset by higher logistics and bunkering costs.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Neither e-fuel has a clear cost edge.

insights.claim: Methanol and ethanol bunkering need limited structural change from today's landscape given their logistical flexibility.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Lower infrastructure risk for these fuels.

insights.claim: Ammonia is the exception: complex handling and potential demand aggregation with power sectors developing ammonia-coal cofiring will determine which ports become ammonia bunkering hubs.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Ammonia hub winners will be ports near power-sector demand.

insights.claim: Shipowners should keep options open through dual-fuel programs and scenario planning, since betting on one pathway risks stranding if regulation or cost favors another.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Optionality premium for dual-fuel tonnage.

insights.claim: In the base case, OCCS retrofits on VLSFO vessels and LNG newbuilds are the most capital-efficient decarbonization play, while the high-penalty case strongly favors investing in new fuels.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Base case favors incremental fossil-linked plays; new-fuel capex is a bet on the penalty.

insights.claim: Investment cases for new fuel infrastructure should be structured across multiple regulatory scenarios rather than a single pathway, since the penalty outcome is unresolved.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Scenario-weighted underwriting is needed.

insights.claim: Vessels last 25 to 30 years and only about 4% of the global fleet is open to change through newbuild decisions each year, so today's engine and fuel choices shape the 2050 fleet.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/anand-veeraraghavan
insights.so_what: Slow fleet turnover creates lock-in and a long adoption lag.
